data.title: EDITORILY: A CENTRALIZED EDITORIAL PROCESS AND PUBLICATION PLATFORM FOR THE NUNTIUM

extracted_concepts.extracted_content: Many still rely on manual or loosely organized processes-paired with shared documents or social media drafts-which can result in workflow confusion, inconsistent revisions, and weak editorial oversight. Along with relying on Social Media for publishing content, though there’s the benefit of a wider reach for content discoverability, it also comes with the issue of having little to no options with preserving content since posted articles in social media have no way to be managed due to the simple fact that Social Media was never built to support what a student publication is made to do-which is to deliver content to its readers in an organized manner.

The study employed a Modified Waterfall Methodology tailored to the academic requirements of the researchers. The development process followed a structured sequence consisting of Requirements and Analysis, System Design, Development, Testing and Evaluation, and Implementation and Maintenance. Purposive Sampling approach was carefully selected to choose participants who possess the appropriate knowledge, expertise, and experience relevant to the study (10 IT Experts, 10 Subject Matter Experts, 10 End Users).

Editorially is a web application made so that Student Publications do not have to rely on Social Media sites alone to deliver their content and practice their journalistic proficiency. Its main purpose is to centralize and streamline the editorial process of student publications. The system is composed of 3 main modules: the Publication Site, Content Pipeline Module, and Article Management Module.

Credibility has long been recognized as the cornerstone of responsible journalism. In an era of digital transformation, however, maintaining that credibility has become increasingly complex (Nabirye H., 2025). Project management systems (PMS) are designed to centralize organizational processes, allowing teams to plan, monitor, and execute tasks efficiently within a unified digital environment (Aliazas et al., 2024).

The system achieved an Overall Mean Score of 4.49 with a Standard Deviation of 0.61, interpreted as “Excellent” using ISO 25010 criteria across IT Experts, Subject Matter Experts, and End Users. The mobile application evaluated using MARS achieved an Overall Mean Score of 3.61, interpreted as “Highly Acceptable.”

concept_relationships.reason: The problems of fragmented workflows and manual processes identified in the student publication directly dictated the application of the Waterfall methodology and purposive sampling of users for development and testing.
The structured requirements analysis, system design phases (Waterfall), and user feedback directly materialized into the development of Editorially and its core modules.
The literature regarding centralized content management systems and project management tools strongly guided the design and functional requirements established in the methodology.
The implemented solution (Editorially web and mobile application) was directly evaluated by users, resulting in the ISO 25010 and MARS evaluation results and performance metrics.
The initial publication problems regarding unorganized publishing and weak oversight were evaluated through testing and user surveys to prove that the system successfully solved these challenges.

The reviewed literature on digital journalism credibility and CMS benefits strongly justified the inclusion of specific features in Editorially, such as approval workflows and a dedicated publication site.

cohesion_analysis.reason: The problem is clearly stated, detailing specific issues faced by student publications such as fragmented workflows, social media reliance, and lack of oversight.
The methodology appropriately links the requirements gathering, Waterfall development phases, and validation methods using defined sampling techniques.
The solution (Editorially web/mobile app) directly corresponds to the stated problems and implements specific modules to solve them.
The literature thoroughly covers digital journalism credibility, challenges of student publications, and the role of content management systems, aligning well with the project's goals.
The results comprehensively present quantitative data from ISO 25010 and MARS evaluations involving IT experts, SMEs, and end-users, directly validating the solution.
